title: Who Is God? The Trinity
subtitle: The one God who has always lived as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and why the church staked its life on getting this right.
triageNote: This is the doctrine that makes Christianity Christianity, confessed in the Nicene Creed. To deny it is not to hold a different opinion inside the faith. It is to describe another religion.
question: When a Christian says the word God, who is being named? Is God a single solitary person who later appeared in different forms, or three separate gods working together, or something the words barely stretch to hold: one God, undivided, who has eternally existed as three who love one another?
whyItMatters:
Start with the new believer who has just prayed for the first time and now wonders who heard. The answer the church gives is not a riddle dropped in to confuse you. It is the most careful thing Christians have ever said, and they said it because the Bible would not let them say anything smaller.

If God were a single person alone before creation, then love is not what God is. Love would be something God only learned to do once there was a world to love. But Scripture says God is love, full stop, before any world existed. That is only true if God has always been more than one who gives and receives love. The Trinity is the reason a Christian can say that the universe was made by love, out of love, for love, and mean every word.

It matters for your salvation too. If Jesus is only the highest creature God ever made, then on the cross a creature died, and a creature cannot carry the weight of the world. Only God can save you, and only a man can stand in your place. The gospel needs Jesus to be both. The Trinity is not theology stacked on top of the good news. It is the good news holding its shape.

positions.name: The Nicene doctrine (orthodox)
positions.inOneLine: There is one God who exists eternally as three coequal, coeternal persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
positions.bestCase:
Begin with what the whole Bible insists on before anything else. There is one God. Deuteronomy 6:4, the verse Israel still prays, says it plainly: the Lord our God, the Lord is one. This conviction has a name. Monotheism means the belief that there is only one God, not many. The church never traded this away. Whatever else gets said about Father, Son, and Spirit, it gets said inside the fence of one God.

And yet the first Christians, all of them Jews who had prayed Deuteronomy 6:4 their whole lives, found themselves praying to Jesus and calling the Spirit God without feeling they had betrayed the one God. They were not being careless. They were following the evidence. So the church reached for words. It said God is one in essence and three in person. Essence, from the Greek word ousia, means what something most deeply is, the very stuff of its being. Person, from the Greek word hypostasis, means a distinct someone, a center of I and you and we. God is one what and three who. The Father is not the Son. The Son is not the Spirit. The Spirit is not the Father. Yet the Father is God, the Son is God, the Spirit is God, and there is one God.

In the year 325, gathered at Nicaea, the church chose one word to guard this and would not let it go: homoousios, of the same substance. The Son is not similar to God or close to God or made by God. The Son is of the very same being as the Father. Whatever it is to be God, the Son is that, without remainder, from eternity. The church also confessed that the Son is eternally generated from the Father, and the Spirit eternally proceeds. Eternal generation means the Son is begotten of the Father not as an event back at the start of time but as an eternal relationship that always was. Procession is the same kind of word for the Spirit, who comes forth from the Father. These are not three ranks. They are three ways of belonging to one another inside the single life of God.

The early teachers gave us one more word to keep the three from drifting apart into a committee. Perichoresis means mutual indwelling, the truth that each person fully lives in the others. The Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father. They are not three roommates sharing an address. They so completely indwell one another that to meet one is to meet the one God. This is why a new believer is not praying to a crowd. You are praying to one God who is, in himself, a fellowship of self-giving love.

Two more terms help you read the rest of this page. The economic Trinity means God as he shows himself to us in what he does in history: the Father sends, the Son saves, the Spirit fills. The immanent Trinity means God as he is in himself, apart from the world, in the life he has always lived. The church learned the second from the first. We watched the Father send the Son and pour out the Spirit, and we trusted that what God shows us of himself is true to who he eternally is.
advocates: the Cappadocian Fathers (Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa)

positions.name: Arianism
positions.inOneLine: The Son is the highest and first of all creatures, glorious beyond every other, but not eternal God.
positions.bestCase:
Hear this as its teacher Arius meant it, because he was no fool and he was trying to protect something real. Arius wanted to guard the oneness and the greatness of God. If God is truly God, Arius reasoned, then God must be utterly unique, unbegotten, without source or beginning. Nothing can share that. To say the Son is God in the same sense would seem to split the one God in two, and Arius would rather die than divide God.

So Arius offered what looked like reverence. The Son, he taught, is the firstborn of all creation, the masterpiece God made before he made anything else, so exalted that through him God made everything else. The Son is higher than angels, worthy of honor, the perfect image of the Father. But there was, Arius said, a time when the Son was not. The Son had a beginning. He is the greatest of creatures, not the Creator.

You can feel why it appealed. It seemed to honor God's uniqueness. It made the verses where Jesus prays to the Father and says the Father is greater easy to read. It kept the math simple: one God, one creation, the Son at the top of the creation. For a person frightened of saying something wild about God, Arianism felt safe.

The church judged it outside the faith, and here is why. If the Son is a creature, then when we worship Jesus we are worshiping a creature, which is idolatry. If the Son had a beginning, then there was a moment when God was a Father with no Son, and God changed, which Scripture denies. Worst of all, a creature cannot save. Only God can bridge the gap between God and us. Athanasius gave his life to this fight precisely because he saw that Arianism, however reverent it sounded, left us unsaved. At Nicaea the church answered with homoousios. Not similar substance. The same. Modern Jehovah's Witnesses hold a teaching close to this older view, which is why their translation renders John 1:1 as the Word was a god.

positions.name: Modalism (Sabellianism)
positions.inOneLine: God is one single person who appears in three different modes or masks: as Father, then as Son, then as Spirit.
positions.bestCase:
This one comes from a good instinct too, and you should respect it. Sabellius and those who taught like him were defending the oneness of God against anyone who seemed to be making three gods. They heard the Trinity language and worried it would crack the one God into pieces. So they offered a tidy solution: God is one person, period, and Father, Son, and Spirit are three roles the one God plays at different times, the way one actor might wear three masks across one play.

In this picture, God was the Father in creation, then became the Son to walk among us and die, then became the Spirit at Pentecost. Same person throughout. No division at all. The word modalism comes from this idea of God acting in three modes.

It appealed because it sounds humble and simple. It guards the oneness with both hands. It lets you say God himself died for you on the cross without any talk of three. For someone who finds three persons dizzying, one person in three costumes feels like relief.

But the church saw what it cost. If Father and Son are just two masks on one person, then the Gospels become theater with no real relationship inside them. When Jesus prays in the garden, who is he talking to: himself? When the Father speaks from heaven at the baptism while the Son stands in the water and the Spirit descends as a dove, all three are present at once, not one after another. The love between the Father and the Son, which John says existed before the world, would be a single person loving himself. The cross would become the Father suffering, a confusion the early church flatly rejected. Modalism saves the oneness by deleting the relationships, and the relationships are the heart of the matter. Today the Oneness Pentecostal movement carries a teaching in this family, sincerely held and worth treating with care.

positions.name: Tritheism
positions.inOneLine: Father, Son, and Spirit are three separate gods who agree perfectly and work as a team.
positions.bestCase:
Few people set out to teach this on purpose, and it has rarely had a famous champion. It tends to be where people land by accident when they take the three persons seriously but lose hold of the one essence. Hear it at its most sincere. Someone reads the Gospels, sees the Father and the Son and the Spirit each acting, each distinct, each fully God, and concludes the honest thing to say is that there are three divine persons who are three Gods, perfectly united in will and love, a family of three.

The pull is real. It takes the threeness with full seriousness and refuses to flatten it. It makes the conversations between Father and Son in the Gospels perfectly natural. It feels concrete where the orthodox answer feels hard to picture. And it tells a warm story: a loving community of divine persons.

The church said no, and gently. The Bible's first and deepest word about God is that he is one, not three who get along. Three gods, however unified, are still three gods, and Scripture's whole spine is monotheism. Israel did not die for a better team of gods than the nations around them. They died for the one God who alone is God. Tritheism keeps the persons and loses the unity, and so it slides from Christianity back toward the very paganism the Bible was given to end. The orthodox answer is harder to hold precisely because it refuses both errors at once: not one person in masks, and not three gods, but one God who is three persons.
advocates: no major intentional teacher, a common informal error, sometimes charged against John Philoponus

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: the oneness of God that every Trinitarian must keep
biblicalEvidence.summary: Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one. This is the bedrock. Whatever the Trinity means, it can never mean more than one God.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Tritheism, which ends with three gods, and anyone who imagines the Trinity loosens monotheism
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Modalists love this verse and read it as proof that God is one solitary person. Orthodoxy answers that the verse insists on one God, one essence, and says nothing requiring God to be only one person. The Hebrew word for one can describe a unity, as when a man and wife become one flesh.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: the full deity and eternity of the Son
biblicalEvidence.summary: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The Son existed in the beginning, was distinct from the Father (with God), and was himself God.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Arianism, because the Word did not begin and is called God outright
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Jehovah's Witnesses translate the last phrase as the Word was a god, making Jesus a lesser divine creature. Orthodoxy responds that the grammar does not demand that reading, that the passage places the Word before all creation, and that verse 3 says all things were made through him, which puts him on the Creator's side of the line, not the creature's.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: the unity of Father and Son in one essence
biblicalEvidence.summary: I and the Father are one. Jesus claims a oneness with the Father so strong that his hearers picked up stones to kill him for blasphemy, understanding him to make himself God.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Arianism and Tritheism, because the union is too deep for a creature or a separate god
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Modalists read this as proof that Father and Son are the same person. Orthodoxy notes Jesus says we are one, not I am he. He names a unity of essence between two who remain distinct, which is exactly the Trinity, not a collapse of the two into one.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: the relationship of Father and Son within the one God
biblicalEvidence.summary: The Father is greater than I. Jesus, having come to do the Father's will, speaks of the Father as greater.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: any view that erases the order and relationship between the persons
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Arians treated this as the master text: the Son is lesser, therefore a creature. Orthodoxy reads it of the Son in his earthly mission, having taken on our flesh and humbled himself, and of the Father as the eternal source from whom the Son is begotten. Greater here speaks of order and origin, not of a difference in being. The same Son says in John 10:30 that he and the Father are one.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: the real humanity of the Son alongside his deity
biblicalEvidence.summary: Concerning that day no one knows, not the angels, nor the Son, but only the Father. Jesus says there is something the Son does not know.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: any neat answer, and a favorite of those who deny the Son's deity
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Arians used this to argue a true God would know everything, so the Son must be less than God. Orthodoxy answers from the two natures of Christ: the Son is fully God and fully man, and in his human mind, accepting the limits of a real human life, he did not access this knowledge. The verse shows how completely God entered our condition, not that the Son is a creature.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: nothing directly about the Son. A wisdom poem later dragged into the debate
biblicalEvidence.summary: The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his way. Wisdom is pictured as present with God before creation, rejoicing before him.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: careful interpreters on all sides, because it is poetry about wisdom, not a doctrinal statement about the Son
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Arians read the Greek as the Lord created me and identified this Wisdom with Christ, making the Son a created being. Orthodoxy answers on two fronts: this is a personification of wisdom in a poem, not a literal claim about the Son, and even if applied to Christ, the underlying word can mean possessed or brought forth rather than created. A poem about wisdom cannot overturn John 1, where the Word is plainly God.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: the three persons named together as one name
biblicalEvidence.summary: Baptize them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. One name, singular, shared by three.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Tritheism, which would need three names, and Modalism, which struggles to explain three at once
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Oneness believers read the singular name as proof of one person and point to Acts, where people are baptized in the name of Jesus. Orthodoxy notes the one name held by three persons is the Trinity in a sentence: not three gods (one name) and not one person (three listed distinctly), but one God in three.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: the eternal glory shared between Father and Son before creation
biblicalEvidence.summary: Father, glorify me with the glory I had with you before the world existed. The Son speaks of a shared glory and a loving relationship that predates the world.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Arianism, since a creature did not share God's glory before creation, and Modalism, since this is one person addressing another
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Modalists must explain how God talks to himself here. Orthodoxy hears exactly what the Trinity describes: the Son, distinct from the Father, asking in real relationship, recalling a glory and a love they shared before anything was made. This is why Christians say love is older than the world.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: the three persons worshiped together as the one God who blesses
biblicalEvidence.summary: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all. Paul blesses the church by all three, side by side, as the single source of grace.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Modalism, since all three are named at once as present, and Arianism, since the Son and Spirit stand alongside God as givers of divine grace
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Most read this simply as a benediction, and it is. Orthodoxy points out how naturally Paul, a strict monotheist, places Father, Son, and Spirit together as the one fountain of blessing, without a hint that he feels he is betraying the one God of Israel. The Trinity is not a later invention. It is already breathing in the earliest letters.

weighing:
On this doctrine the church does not offer you a menu. It offers you a confession. The Nicene answer is not one orthodox option among several. It is the line that marks where Christianity is and where it stops being Christianity. That is why this page is written differently from a page on baptism or the end times. The burden of proof here is crushing for anyone who wants to move the line, and it should be. Twenty centuries of the church, across every continent and tradition, East and West, Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant, confess one God in three persons. A new believer can rest in that with both feet. You are not betting on a fragile theory. You are standing where the whole church has always stood.

That said, honesty requires naming the questions that remain genuinely open among Christians who all confess Nicaea fully. These are family questions, asked inside the house, not arguments about whether the house should stand. The first concerns the Holy Spirit. The filioque, a Latin word meaning and the Son, is a phrase the Western church added to the Nicene Creed, saying the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. The Eastern church kept the original wording, that the Spirit proceeds from the Father. Both sides confess the full deity of the Spirit. They differ on how to describe his eternal procession, and that difference, layered with old wounds, runs along the line between East and West. It is a second-order question, weighty but not the line between faith and unbelief.

The second open question is newer. Some recent theologians have argued for what they call the eternal functional subordination of the Son, the idea that the Son eternally submits to the Father in role while remaining fully equal in being. Others answer that this language risks reopening the door Nicaea closed and that the older account of eternal generation already explains the order among the persons without ranking their authority. This debate is live among careful, orthodox Christians right now, and a new believer is not required to settle it to be on solid ground. Hold the Nicene center with conviction, and hold these inside questions with humility, knowing that good Christians who love the same Lord still reason their way to different answers.
charitableDisagreement:
When you talk with a Jehovah's Witness at your door, a Oneness Pentecostal cousin who loves Jesus deeply, or an Eastern Orthodox believer with fifteen centuries of prayer behind her, lead with the truth that each of them is reaching for something real. The Jehovah's Witness wants to guard the one God. The Oneness believer wants to guard the one God too, and wants the cross to be God himself dying for you. The Eastern Orthodox believer already shares the entire Nicene faith with you and differs only on one clause about the Spirit. Begin where they are right, ask questions before you correct, and read the hard verses together rather than firing them across the table. Most people who land in these views were never shown how John 1:1 and Deuteronomy 6:4 hold together at once, and a patient walk through the texts does more than a debate ever will. Treat heresy the way a physician treats a wound, with clear eyes and steady hands, never with mockery.

Now the hill, because not every line is the same. With the Eastern Orthodox believer, the filioque is real but it is not a hill to die on. You already confess the same triune God, and you can take communion in the same hope. With the Jehovah's Witness and the Oneness Pentecostal, you have arrived at the hill itself, gently but truly. Whether Jesus is the eternal God, of the same substance as the Father, and whether God is truly three persons and not one in masks, are not negotiable details. They decide whether the God being worshiped is the God who made and saved the world. Say it without heat and without flinching: the deity of Christ and the tri-personal life of the one God are the ground we stand on, and everyone is welcome to come and stand on it, but it does not move.

relatedDebates.topic: The filioque and the East-West split
relatedDebates.note: Whether the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or from the Father and the Son. The West added and the Son to the creed, while the East kept the original. A second-order line between two traditions that share the full Nicene faith, freighted with a thousand years of history.

relatedDebates.topic: Eternal functional subordination of the Son
relatedDebates.note: A live debate among orthodox Protestants over whether the Son eternally submits to the Father in role while remaining equal in being, or whether such language strains against Nicaea and the older grammar of eternal generation already says everything that needs saying.

Water as ice, liquid, and steam slips into Modalism, since the same water merely changes form. The three parts of an egg, or the three leaves of a shamrock, slide toward Tritheism, since shell and white and yolk are three separate pieces, not one God. Every physical picture breaks because God is unlike anything made. The persons are best known not by analogy but by watching the Father send the Son and pour out the Spirit in the Gospels.
